entries.91a17416b8b8139bcf7a6b3cb71c46e912cfeecd: <div sID="gen18057" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="42" osisID="Jer.42" sID="Jer.42"/> <div eID="gen18057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18058" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18059" type="x-p"/> Johanan and the captains being strongly bent upon going into Egypt, either their affections or politics advising them to take that course, they had a great desire that God should direct them to do so too like Balaam, who, when he was determined to go and curse Israel, asked God leave. Here is, I. The fair bargain that was made between Jeremiah and them about consulting God in this matter, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.1-Jer.42.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. The message at large which God sent them, in answer to their enquiry, in which, 1. They are commanded and encouraged to continue in the land of Judah, and assured that if they did so it should be well with them, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.7-Jer.42.12">ver. 7-12</reference>. 2. They are forbidden to go to Egypt, and are plainly told that if they did it would be their ruin, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.13-Jer.42.18">ver. 13-18</reference>. 3. They are charged with dissimulation in their asking what God's will was in this matter and disobedience when they were told what it was; and sentence is accordingly passed upon them, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.19-Jer.42.22">ver. 19-22</reference>.
entries.98c468f418c9d06dddaa14ceeface4069a63e8e6: <div eID="gen18059" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18058" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Jeremiah Agrees to Consult God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18060" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then all the captains of the forces, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least even unto the greatest, came near, <hi type="super">2</hi> And said unto Jeremiah the prophet, Let, we beseech thee, our supplication be accepted before thee, and pray for us unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, <hi type="italic">even</hi> for all this remnant; (for we are left <hi type="italic">but</hi> a few of many, as thine eyes do behold us:) <hi type="super">3</hi> That the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God may shew us the way wherein we may walk, and the thing that we may do. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then Jeremiah the prophet said unto them, I have heard <hi type="italic">you;</hi> behold, I will pray unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God according to your words; and it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> whatsoever thing the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall answer you, I will declare <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto you; I will keep nothing back from you. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then they said to Jeremiah, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> be a true and faithful witness between us, if we do not even according to all things for the which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God shall send thee to us. <hi type="super">6</hi> Whether <hi type="italic">it be</hi> good, or whether <hi type="italic">it be</hi> evil, we will obey the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God, to whom we send thee; that it may be well with us, when we obey the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God. <div eID="gen18060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18061" type="x-p"/> We have reason to wonder how Jeremiah the prophet escaped the sword of Ishmael; it seems he did escape, and it was not the first time that the Lord hid him. It is strange also that in these violent turns he was not consulted before now, and his advice asked and taken. But it should seem as if they knew not that a prophet was among them. Though this people were <hi type="italic">as brands plucked out of the fire,</hi> yet have they not <hi type="italic">returned to the Lord.</hi> This people has a <hi type="italic">revolting and a rebellious heart;</hi> and contempt of God and his providence, God and his prophets, is still <hi type="italic">the sin that most easily besets</hi> them. But now at length, to serve a turn, Jeremiah is sought out, and <hi type="italic">all the captains, Johanan</hi> himself not excepted, with <hi type="italic">all the people from the least to the greatest,</hi> make him a visit; they <hi type="italic">came near</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.1">v. 1</reference>), which intimates that hitherto they had kept at a distance from the prophet and had been shy of him. Now here, <div eID="gen18061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18062" type="x-p"/> I. They desire him by prayer to ask direction from God what they should do in the present critical juncture, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.2-Jer.42.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. They express themselves wonderfully well. 1. With great respect to the prophet. Though he was poor and low, and under their command, yet they apply to him with humility and submissiveness, as petitioners for his assistance, which yet they intimate their own unworthiness of: <hi type="italic">Let, we beseech thee, our supplication be accepted before thee.</hi> They compliment him thus in hopes to persuade him to say as they would have him say. 2. With a great opinion of his interest in heaven: "<hi type="italic">Pray for us,</hi> who know not how to pray for ourselves. <hi type="italic">Pray to the Lord thy God,</hi> for we are unworthy to call him ours, nor have we reason to expect any favour from him." 3. With a great sense of their need of divine direction. They speak of themselves as objects of compassion: "<hi type="italic">We are but a remnant, but a few of many;</hi> how easily will such a remnant be swallowed up, and yet it is a pity that it should. <hi type="italic">Thy eyes</hi> see what distress we are in, what a plunge we are at; if thou canst do any thing, help us." 4. With desire of divine direction: "Let <hi type="italic">the Lord thy God</hi> take this ruin into his thoughts and under his hand, and <hi type="italic">show us the way wherein we may walk</hi> and may expect to have his presence with us, <hi type="italic">and the thing that we may do,</hi> the course we may take for our own safety." Note, In every difficult doubtful case our eye must be up to God for direction. They then might expect to be directed by a <hi type="italic">spirit of prophecy,</hi> which has now ceased; but we may still in faith pray to be guided by a <hi type="italic">spirit of wisdom</hi> in our hearts and the hints of Providence. <div eID="gen18062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18063" type="x-p"/> II. Jeremiah faithfully promises them to pray for direction for them, and, whatever message God should send to them by him, he would deliver it to them just as he received it without adding, altering, or diminishing, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.4">v. 4</reference>. Ministers may hence learn, 1. Conscientiously to pray for those who desire their prayers: <hi type="italic">I will pray for you according to your words.</hi> Though they had slighted him, yet, like Samuel when he was slighted, he will not <hi type="italic">sin against the Lord in ceasing to pray for</hi> them, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.23">1 Sam. xii. 23</reference>. 2. Conscientiously to advise those who desire their advice as near as they can to the mind of God, not <hi type="italic">keeping back any thing that is profitable for them,</hi> whether it be pleasing or no, but to <hi type="italic">declare to them the whole counsel of God,</hi> that they may approve themselves true to their trust. <div eID="gen18063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18064" type="x-p"/> III. They fairly promise that they will be governed by the will of God, as soon as they know what it is (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.5-Jer.42.6">v. 5, 6</reference>), and they had the impudence to appeal to God concerning their sincerity herein, though at the same time they dissembled: "<hi type="italic">The Lord be a true and faithful witness between us;</hi> do thou in the fear of God tell us truly what his mind is and then we will in the fear of God comply with it, and for this the Lord the Judge be Judge between us." Note, Those that expect to have the benefit of good ministers' prayers must conscientiously hearken to their preaching and be governed by it, as far as it agrees with the mind of God. Nothing could be better than this was: <hi type="italic">Whether it be good, or whether it be evil, we will obey the voice of the Lord our God, that it may be well with us.</hi> 1. They now call God <hi type="italic">their</hi> God, for Jeremiah had encouraged them to call him so (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will pray to the Lord your God.</hi> He is ours, and therefore <hi type="italic">we will obey his voice.</hi> Our relation to God strongly obliges us to obedience. 2. They promise to <hi type="italic">obey his voice</hi> because they sent the prophet to him to consult him. Note, We do not truly desire to know the mind of God if we do not fully resolve to comply with it when we do know it. 3. It is an implicit universal obedience that they here promise. They will do what God appoints them to do, <hi type="italic">whether it be good or whether it be evil:</hi> "Though it may seem evil to us, yet we will believe that if God command it it is certainly good, and we must not dispute it, but do it. Whatever God commands, whether it be easy or difficult, agreeable to our inclinations or contrary to them, whether it be cheap or costly, fashionable or unfashionable, whether we get or lose by it in our worldly interests, if it be our duty, we will do it." 4. It is upon a very good consideration that they promise this, a reasonable and powerful one, <hi type="italic">that it may be well with us,</hi> which intimates a conviction that they could not expect it should be well with them upon any other terms.
entries.c2652c39955e2d331ae71d5303eff85a3fa14d34: <div eID="gen18064" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jeremiah's Address to the People. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18065" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And it came to pass after ten days, that the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto <reference osisRef="Jer.8">Jeremiah.   8</reference> Then called he Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces which <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, and all the people from the least even to the greatest, <hi type="super">9</hi> And said unto them, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of Israel, unto whom ye sent me to present your supplication before him; <hi type="super">10</hi> If ye will still abide in this land, then will I build you, and not pull <hi type="italic">you</hi> down, and I will plant you, and not pluck <hi type="italic">you</hi> up: for I repent me of the evil that I have done unto you. <hi type="super">11</hi> Be not afraid of the king of Babylon, of whom ye are afraid; be not afraid of him, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> with you to save you, and to deliver you from his hand. <hi type="super">12</hi> And I will shew mercies unto you, that he may have mercy upon you, and cause you to return to your own land. <hi type="super">13</hi> But if ye say, We will not dwell in this land, neither obey the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, <hi type="super">14</hi> Saying, No; but we will go into the land of Egypt, where we shall see no war, nor hear the sound of the trumpet, nor have hunger of bread; and there will we dwell: <hi type="super">15</hi> And now therefore hear the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , ye remnant of Judah; Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; If ye wholly set your faces to enter into Egypt, and go to sojourn there; <hi type="super">16</hi> Then it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the sword, which ye feared, shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt, and the famine, whereof ye were afraid, shall follow close after you there in Egypt; and there ye shall die. <hi type="super">17</hi> So shall it be with all the men that set their faces to go into Egypt to sojourn there; they shall die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence: and none of them shall remain or escape from the evil that I will bring upon them. <hi type="super">18</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; As mine anger and my fury hath been poured forth upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem; so shall my fury be poured forth upon you, when ye shall enter into Egypt: and ye shall be an execration, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach; and ye shall see this place no more. <hi type="super">19</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath said concerning you, O ye remnant of Judah; Go ye not into Egypt: know certainly that I have admonished you this day. <hi type="super">20</hi> For ye dissembled in your hearts, when ye sent me unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, saying, Pray for us unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God; and according unto all that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God shall say, so declare unto us, and we will do <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">21</hi> And <hi type="italic">now</hi> I have this day declared <hi type="italic">it</hi> to you; but ye have not obeyed the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God, nor any <hi type="italic">thing</hi> for the which he hath sent me unto you. <hi type="super">22</hi> Now therefore know certainly that ye shall die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence, in the place whither ye desire to go <hi type="italic">and</hi> to sojourn. <div eID="gen18065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18066" type="x-p"/> We have here the answer which Jeremiah was sent to deliver to those who employed him to ask counsel of God. <div eID="gen18066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18067" type="x-p"/> I. It did not come immediately, not till <hi type="italic">ten days after,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.42.7">v. 7</reference>. They were thus long held in suspense, perhaps, to punish them for their hypocrisy or to show that Jeremiah did not speak of himself, nor what he would, for he could not speak when he would, but must wait for instructions. However, it teaches us to continue waiting upon God for direction in our way. <hi type="italic">The vision is for an appointed time, and at the end it shall speak.</hi> <div eID="gen18067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18068" type="x-p"/> II. When it did come he delivered it publicly, both to the <hi type="italic">captains</hi> and to all the <hi type="italic">people,</hi> from the meanest to those in the highest station; he delivered it fully and faithfully as he received it, as he had promised that he would keep nothing back from them. If Jeremiah had been to direct them by his own prudence, perhaps he could not have told what to advise them to, the case was so difficult; but what he has to advise is what <hi type="italic">the Lord the God of Israel saith,</hi> to whom they had sent him, and therefore they were bound in honour and duty to observe it. And this he tells them, <div eID="gen18068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18069" type="x-p"/> 1. That it is the will of God that they should stay where they are, and his promise that, if they do so, it shall undoubtedly be <hi type="italic">well with them</hi> he would have them still to <hi type="italic">abide in this land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.42.10">v. 10</reference>. Their brethren were forced out of it into captivity, and this was their affliction; let those therefore count it a mercy that they may stay in it and a duty to stay in it. Let those whose lot is in Canaan never quit it while they can keep it. It would have been enough to oblige them if God had only said, "I charge you upon your allegiance to <hi type="italic">abide still in the land;</hi>" but he rather persuades them to it as a friend than commands it as a prince. (1.) He expresses a very tender concern for them in their present calamitous condition: <hi type="italic">It repenteth me of the evil that I have done unto you.</hi> Though they had shown small sign of their repenting of their sins, yet God, as one <hi type="italic">grieved for the misery of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.10.16">Judg. x. 16</reference>), begins to repent of the judgments he had brought upon them for their sins. Not that he changed his mind, but he was very ready to change his way and to return in mercy to them. God's time to repent himself concerning his servants is when he sees that, as here, their strength is gone, and <hi type="italic">there is none shut up or left,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.36">Deut. xxxii. 36</reference>. (2.) He answers the argument they had against abiding in this land. <hi type="italic">They feared the king of Babylon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.41.18">ch. xli. 18</reference>), lest he should come and avenge the death of Gedaliah upon them, though they were no way accessory to it, nay, had witnessed against it. The surmise was foreign and unreasonable; but, if there had been any ground for it, enough is here said to remove it (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Be not afraid of the king of Babylon,</hi> though he is a man of great might and little mercy, and a very arbitrary prince, whose will is a law, and therefore you are afraid he will upon this pretence, though without colour of reason, take advantage against you; <hi type="italic">be not afraid of him,</hi> for that fear will bring a snare: fear not him, for <hi type="italic">I am with you;</hi> and, if God be for you to save you, who can be against you to hurt you?" Thus has God provided to obviate and silence even the causeless fears of his people, which discourage them in the way of their duty; there is enough in the promises to encourage them. (3.) He assures them that if they will still abide in this land they shall not only be safe from the king of Babylon, but be made happy by the King of kings: "<hi type="italic">I will build you and plant you;</hi> you shall take root again, and be the new foundation of another state, a phoenix-kingdom, rising out of the ashes of the last." It is added (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.12">v. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will show mercies unto you.</hi> Note, In all our comforts we may read God's mercies. God will show them mercy in this, that not only the king of Babylon shall not destroy them, but he shall <hi type="italic">have mercy upon them</hi> and help to settle them. Note, Whatever kindness men do us we must attribute it to God's kindness. He makes those whom he pities to be pitied even by <hi type="italic">those who carried them captives,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.16.46">Ps. xvi. 46</reference>. "The king of Babylon, having now the disposal of the country, shall <hi type="italic">cause you to return it to your own land,</hi> shall settle you again in your own habitations and put you in possession of the lands that formerly belonged to you." Note, God has made that our duty which is really our privilege, and our obedience will be its own recompence. "<hi type="italic">Abide in this land,</hi> and it shall be your own land again and you shall continue in it. Do not quit it now that you stand so fair for the enjoyment of it again. Be no so unwise as to <hi type="italic">forsake your own mercies</hi> for <hi type="italic">lying vanities.</hi>" <div eID="gen18069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18070" type="x-p"/> 2. That as they tender the favour of God and their own happiness they must by no means think of going into Egypt, not thither of all places, not to that land out of which God had delivered their fathers and which he had so often warned them not to make alliance with nor to put confidence in. Observe here, (1.) The sin they are supposed to be guilty of (and to him that knew their hearts it was more than a supposition): "You begin to say, <hi type="italic">We will not dwell in this land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.13">v. 13</reference>); we will never think that we can be safe in it, no, not though God himself undertake our protection. We will not continue in it, no, not <hi type="italic">in obedience to the voice of the Lord our God.</hi> He may say what he please, but we will do what we please. We will <hi type="italic">go into the land of Egypt,</hi> and <hi type="italic">there will we dwell,</hi> whether God give us leave and go along with us or no," <reference osisRef="Jer.42.14">v. 14</reference>. It is supposed that their hearts were upon it: "<hi type="italic">If you wholly set your faces to enter into Egypt,</hi> and are obstinately resolved that you will go and <hi type="italic">sojourn there,</hi> though God oppose you in it both by his word and by his providence, then take what follows." Now the reason they go upon in this resolution is that "<hi type="italic">in Egypt we shall see no war, nor have hunger of bread,; as we have had for a long time in this land," <reference osisRef="Jer.42.14">v. 14</reference>. Note, It is folly to quit our place, especially to quit the holy land, because we meet with trouble in it; but greater folly to think by changing our place to escape the judgments of God, and that evil which pursues sinners in every way of disobedience, and which there is no escaping but by returning to our allegiance. (2.) The sentence passed upon them for this sin, if they will persist in it. It is pronounced in God's name (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.15">v. 15</reference>): "Hear the word of the Lord, you remnant of Judah,</hi> who think that because you are a remnant you must be spared of course (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.2">v. 2</reference>) and indulged in your own humour." [1.] Did the sword and famine frighten them? Those very judgments shall pursue them into Egypt, shall overtake them, and overcome them there (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.16-Jer.42.17">v. 16, 17</reference>): "You think, because war and famine have long been raging in this land, that they are entailed upon it; whereas, if you trust in God, he can make even this land a land of peace to you; you think they are confined to it, and, if you can get clear of this land, you shall get out of the reach of them, but God will send them after you wherever you go." Note, the evils we think to escape by sin we certainly and inevitably run ourselves upon. The men that go to Egypt in contradiction to God's will, to escape <hi type="italic">the sword and famine,</hi> shall <hi type="italic">die in Egypt by sword and famine.</hi> We may apply it to the common calamities of human life; those that are impatient of them, and think to avoid them by changing their place, will find that they are deceived and that they do not at all better themselves. The grievances common to men will meet them wherever they go. All our removes in this world are but from one wilderness to another; still we are where we were. [2.] Did the desolations of Jerusalem frighten them? Were they willing to get as far as they could from them? They shall meet with the second part of them too in Egypt (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">As my anger and fury have been poured out</hi> here upon Jerusalem, so they shall be <hi type="italic">poured out upon you in Egypt.</hi> Note, Those that have by sin made God their enemy will find him a consuming fire wherever they go. And then you shall be <hi type="italic">an execration and an astonishment.</hi> The Hebrews were of old an abomination to the Egyptians (<reference osisRef="Gen.43.32">Gen. xliii. 32</reference>), and now they shall be made more so than ever. When God's professing people mingle with infidels, and make their court to them, they lose their dignity and make themselves a reproach. <div eID="gen18070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18071" type="x-p"/> 3. That God knew their hypocrisy in their enquiries of him, and that when they asked what he would have them to do they were resolved to take their own way; and therefore the sentence which was before pronounced conditionally is made absolute. Having set before them good and evil, the blessing and the curse, in the close he makes application of what he had said. And here, (1.) He solemnly protests that he had faithfully delivered his message, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.19">v. 19</reference>. The conclusion of the whole matter is, "<hi type="italic">Go not down into Egypt;</hi> you disobey the command of God if you do, and what I have said to you will be a witness against you; for <hi type="italic">know certainly</hi> that, <hi type="italic">whether you will hear or whether you will forbear,</hi> I have plainly <hi type="italic">admonished you;</hi> you cannot now plead ignorance of the mind of God." (2.) He charges them with base dissimulation in the application they made to him for divine direction (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You dissembled in your hearts;</hi> you professed one thing and intended another, promising what you never meant to perform." <hi type="italic">You have used deceit against your soul</hi> (so the margin reads it); for those that think to put a cheat upon God will prove in the end to have put a damning cheat upon themselves. (3.) He is already aware that they are determined to go contrary to the command of God; probably they discovered it in their countenance and secret mutterings already, before he had finished his discourse. However, he spoke from him who knew their hearts: "<hi type="italic">You have not obeyed the voice of the Lord your God;</hi> you have not a disposition to obey it." Thus Moses, in the close of his farewell sermon, had told them (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.27">Deut. xxxi. 27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.29">29</reference>), <hi type="italic">I know thy rebellion and thy stiff neck,</hi> and <hi type="italic">that you will corrupt yourselves.</hi> Admire the patience of God, that he is pleased to speak to those who, he knows, will not regard him, and deal with those who, he knows, will <hi type="italic">deal very treacherously,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.48.8">Isa. xlviii. 8</reference>. (4.) He therefore reads them their doom, ratifying what he had said before: <hi type="italic">Know certainly that you shall die by the sword,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.42.22">v. 22</reference>. God's threatenings may be vilified, but cannot be nullified, by the unbelief of man. <hi type="italic">Famine and pestilence</hi> shall pursue these sinners; for there is no place privileged from divine arrests, nor can any malefactors go out of God's jurisdiction. <hi type="italic">You shall die in the place whither you desire to go.</hi> Note, We know not what is good for ourselves; and that often proves afflictive, and sometimes fatal, which we are most fond of and have our hearts most set upon.  <chapter eID="Jer.42"/> <div eID="gen18071" type="x-p"/>

entries.1adefb84fe7e5e677e7663fb555ad83542e9d4fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10497"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 42</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.42.1-Jer.42.22">Jr 42:1-22</reference>. The Jews and Johanan Inquire of God, through Jeremiah, as to Going to Egypt, Promising Obedience to His Will. Their Safety on Condition of Staying in Judea, and Their Destruction in the Event of Going to Egypt, Are Foretold. Their Hypocrisy in Asking for Counsel Which They Meant Not to Follow, if Contrary to Their Own Determination, Is Reproved.</title> <div sID="gen18715" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10497"/><hi type="bold">2. Jeremiah--</hi>He probably was one of the number carried off from Mizpah, and dwelt with Johanan (<reference osisRef="Jer.41.16">Jr 41:16</reference>). Hence the expression is, "came near" (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.1">Jr 42:1</reference>), not "sent."<div eID="gen18715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18716" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Let ... supplication be accepted--</hi>literally, "fall" (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.36.7">Jr 36:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.37.20">Jr 37:20</reference>).<div eID="gen18716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18717" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pray for us--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.20.7">Ge 20:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.4">Is 37:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.16">Jas 5:16</reference>).<div eID="gen18717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy God--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.42.5">Jr 42:5</reference>). The Jews use this form to express their belief in the peculiar relation in which Jeremiah stood to God as His accredited prophet. Jeremiah in his reply reminds them that God is their God ("your God") as well as his as being the covenant people (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.4">Jr 42:4</reference>). They in turn acknowledge this in <reference osisRef="Jer.42.6">Jr 42:6</reference>, "the Lord our God."<div eID="gen18718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18719" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">few of many--</hi>as had been foretold (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.22">Le 26:22</reference>). <div eID="gen18719" type="x-p"/>
entries.60f04d02038bb184a3eeb66f5996cf5255391d67: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10498"/><div sID="gen18720" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10498"/>3. They consulted God, like many, not so much to know what was right, as wishing Him to authorize what they had already determined on, whether agreeable to His will or not. So Ahab in consulting Micaiah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.13">1Ki 22:13</reference>). Compare Jeremiah's answer (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.4">Jr 42:4</reference>) with Micaiah's (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.14">1Ki 22:14</reference>). <div eID="gen18720" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2ae2ca682716cffde6f8193f68f530de4d7a7f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10499"/><div sID="gen18721" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10499"/><hi type="bold">4. I have heard--</hi>that is, I accede to your request.<div eID="gen18721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18722" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your God--</hi>Being His by adoption, ye are not your own, and are bound to whatever He wills (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Ex 19:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.19">1Co 6:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.20">20</reference>).<div eID="gen18722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">answer you--</hi>that is, through me.<div eID="gen18723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18724" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">keep nothing back--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Sam.3.18">1Sa 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.20">Ac 20:20</reference>). <div eID="gen18724" type="x-p"/>
entries.534a4ab0bbe78d0cee2c8abc5ccad1f0ec09be43: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10500"/><div sID="gen18725" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10500"/><hi type="bold">5. Lord be a true ... witness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.31.50">Ge 31:50</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.37">Psa 89:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Re 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.14">3:14</reference>; 19:11). <div eID="gen18725" type="x-p"/>
entries.995b0944485a790ee329edcd57dc5e82d7fe67a5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10501"/><div sID="gen18726" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10501"/><hi type="bold">6. evil--</hi>not moral evil, which God cannot command (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.13">Jas 1:13</reference>), but what may be disagreeable and hard to us. Piety obeys God, without questioning, at all costs. See the instance defective in this, that it obeyed only so far as was agreeable to itself (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.3">1Sa 15:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.13-1Sam.9.15">9, 13-15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.20-1Sam.9.23">20-23</reference>). <div eID="gen18726" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff8a9dbf950c07d43109f50592ebdc590b459b44: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10502"/><div sID="gen18727" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10502"/><hi type="bold">7. ten days--</hi>Jeremiah did not speak of himself, but waited God's time and revelation, showing the reality of his inspiration. Man left to himself would have given an immediate response to the people, who were impatient of delay. The delay was designed to test the sincerity of their professed willingness to obey, and that they should have full time to deliberate (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.2">De 8:2</reference>). True obedience bows to God's time, as well as His way and will. <div eID="gen18727" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f2b41173b01f7eecc6b4ce0d3e02ad9e51fc443: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10503"/><div sID="gen18728" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10503"/><hi type="bold">10. If ye ... abide--</hi>namely, under the Babylonian authority, to which God hath appointed that all should be subject (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.37">Da 2:37</reference>, 38). To resist was to resist God.<div eID="gen18728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18729" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">build ... plant--</hi>metaphor for, I will firmly establish you (<reference osisRef="Jer.24.6">Jr 24:6</reference>).<div eID="gen18729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I repent ... of the evil--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.18.8">Jr 18:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.36">De 32:36</reference>). I am satisfied with the punishment I have inflicted on you, if only you add not a new offense [Grotius]. God is said to "repent," when He alters His outward ways of dealing. <div eID="gen18730" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb968f5ed87df3300487982c0ecfba95edcda967: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10504"/><div sID="gen18731" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10504"/><hi type="bold">12. show mercies--</hi>rather, I will excite (in him) feelings of mercy towards you [Calvin].<div eID="gen18731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18732" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cause you to return--</hi>permit you to return to the peaceable enjoyment of the possessions from which you are wishing to withdraw through fear of the Chaldeans. By departing in disobedience they should incur the very evils they wished thereby to escape; and by staying they should gain the blessings which they feared to lose by doing so. <div eID="gen18732" type="x-p"/>
entries.888d68ba9d3f0ed6185edc3f3ced14ad0ee4246b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10505"/><div sID="gen18733" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10505"/><hi type="bold">13. if ye say, &c.--</hi>avowed rebellion against God, who had often (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.16">De 17:16</reference>), as now, forbidden their going to Egypt, lest they should be entangled in its idolatry. <div eID="gen18733" type="x-p"/>
entries.a64b56ce396891ba6ee99006d287a2441469c068: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10506"/><div sID="gen18734" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10506"/><hi type="bold">14. where we shall see no war--</hi>Here they betray their impiety in not believing God's promise (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.10">Jr 42:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.11">11</reference>), as if He were a liar (<reference osisRef="1John.5.10">1Jo 5:10</reference>). <div eID="gen18734" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2dabcc62f61c672fc16f55a6b6d49aa62d1973d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10507"/><div sID="gen18735" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10507"/><hi type="bold">15. wholly set your faces--</hi>firmly resolve (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.51">Lu 9:51</reference>) in spite of all warnings (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.12">Jr 44:12</reference>). <div eID="gen18735" type="x-p"/>
entries.729bedc1a8ec554720a89c8cba4e9e33cb31b002: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10508"/><div sID="gen18736" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10508"/><hi type="bold">16. sword, which ye feared, shall overtake you--</hi>The very evils we think to escape by sin, we bring on ourselves thereby. What our hearts are most set on often proves fatal to us. Those who think to escape troubles by changing their place will find them wherever they go (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.8">Eze 11:8</reference>). The "sword" here is that of Nebuchadnezzar, who fulfilled the prediction in his expedition to Africa (according to Megasthenes, a heathen writer), 300 B.C. <div eID="gen18736" type="x-p"/>
entries.35b234b202191bbfdc37fd2f6602a2f2e34d77d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10509"/><div sID="gen18737" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10509"/><hi type="bold">17. all the men--</hi>excepting the "small number" mentioned (<reference osisRef="Jer.44.14">Jr 44:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.28">28</reference>); namely, those who were forced into Egypt against their will, Jeremiah, Baruch, &c., and those who took Jeremiah's advice and fled from Egypt before the arrival of the Chaldeans. <div eID="gen18737" type="x-p"/>
entries.28c14bfb734c27836d8777cccf23d3494452905c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10510"/><div sID="gen18738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10510"/><hi type="bold">18. As mine anger, &c.--</hi>As ye have already, to your sorrow, found Me true to My word, so shall ye again (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.20">Jr 7:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.16">18:16</reference>).<div eID="gen18738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall see this place no more--</hi>Ye shall not return to Judea, as those shall who have been removed to Babylon. <div eID="gen18739" type="x-p"/>
entries.e38f586d6ee4d737b5cbdcbc78cb4742b4a4516b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10511"/><div sID="gen18740" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10511"/><hi type="bold">19. I have admonished--</hi>literally, "testified," that is, solemnly admonished, having yourselves as My witnesses; so that if ye perish, ye yourselves will have to confess that it was through your own fault, not through ignorance, ye perished. <div eID="gen18740" type="x-p"/>
entries.51ac281ead3ca4d8029edd24e9ecd7caa96c60ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10512"/><div sID="gen18741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10512"/><hi type="bold">20. dissembled in your hearts--</hi>rather, "ye have used deceit against your (own) souls." It is not God, but yourselves, whom ye deceive, to your own ruin, by your own dissimulation (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.7">Ga 6:7</reference>) [Calvin]. But the words following accord best with English Version, ye have dissembled in your hearts (see on <reference osisRef="Jer.42.3">Jr 42:3</reference>) towards me, when ye sent me to consult God for you. <div eID="gen18741" type="x-p"/>
entries.74908cada293aff620225edf293cb9e36bb35792: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10513"/><div sID="gen18742" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10513"/><hi type="bold">21. declared it--</hi>namely, the divine will.<div eID="gen18742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18743" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I ... but ye--</hi>antithesis. I have done my part; but ye do not yours. It is no fault of mine that ye act not rightly. <div eID="gen18743" type="x-p"/>
entries.23e2a5b03e6700851fac43a564e4c2f82047f250: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10514"/><div sID="gen18744" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10514"/><hi type="bold">22. sojourn--</hi>for a time, until they could return to their country. They expected, therefore, to be restored, in spite of God's prediction to the contrary. <chapter eID="Jer.42"/>

entries.8494e0cc24a45447034d30b48383d8fde75a3aee: <div eID="gen30438" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30439" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30440" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30440" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30439" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen30441" type="x-p"/> Johanan and the remnant of the people desire Jeremiah to ask counsel of God what they should do, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.1-Jer.42.3">Jer 42:1-3</reference>. The prophet assures them of safety in Judea, but destruction in Egypt, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.4-Jer.42.18">Jer 42:4-18</reference>; and reproves their hypocrisy in asking counsel with which they had no intention to comply, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.19-Jer.42.22">Jer 42:19-22</reference>. <div eID="gen30441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30442" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30443" type="x-p"/> The captains of the forces - The different leaders of the small bands or companies, collected from different parts of the land. The principal are those here named.
entries.4b9348494c619f6d2a4599457183cf30726841fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen30443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30444" type="x-p"/> That the Lord thy God may show us - They all thought there was no safety in Jerusalem or in Judea, and therefore determined to leave the land: but they did not know which might be the safest direction to take; for though they inclined to Egypt, yet they wished to know the mind of God on that point.
entries.b5890d520819e618de1ee5ee8290d2c5baa7e287: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen30444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30445" type="x-p"/> The Lord be a true and faithful Witness - The Lord is such; and as ye have bound yourselves to obey his voice, he will register the covenant, and bless or curse according as ye shall conduct yourselves in this matter.
entries.a2abf364d4aa1a36df420fd31480f9715244fced: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen30445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30446" type="x-p"/> After ten days - All this time he was waiting upon God; for it is evident the prophets could not prophesy when they pleased, any more than the disciples of our Lord could work miracles when they wished. The gift of prophecy and the gift of miracles were both dependent on the will of the Most High, and each of them was given only for the moment; and when the necessity was over, the influence ceased.
entries.3c38b26ca2b005f72283a4a617c62540b2b270fa: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen30446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30447" type="x-p"/> For I repent me of the evil - The meaning is, As I have punished you only because you continued to be rebellious, I will arrest this punishment as soon as you become obedient to my word. You need not fear the king of Babylon if you have me for your helper; and I will so show mercy to you that he shall see it, and cease from afflicting you, as he shall see that I am on your side.
entries.efc32295688bed9cd16fafc102085983ec1799fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen30447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30448" type="x-p"/> If ye - set your faces to enter into Egypt, etc - Every evil that ye dreaded by staying in your own land shall come upon you in Egypt.
entries.a524611666c4a1279c7f0128c0c95035aef6e91f: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen30448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30449" type="x-p"/> The sword - and the famine - shall follow close after you - Shall be at your heels; shall overtake and destroy you; for there ye shall die.
entries.35ecb727052e166df6bd3c7f35a989adc5312858: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen30449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30450" type="x-p"/> Go ye not into Egypt - Why? Because God knew, such was their miserable propensity to idolatry, that they would there adopt the worship of the country, and serve idols.
entries.d127c7523e769ba69a3c9873247ca77a28eb0ce6: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen30450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30451" type="x-p"/> For ye dissembled in your hearts - What a most miserable and incorrigible people! Ingratitude, hypocrisy, rebellion, and cruelty seem to have been enthroned in their hearts! And what are they still? Just what their fathers were, except in the mere article of idolatry; and that they do not practice because they are indifferent to their own religion and to that of all others. Examine their devotions and their lives, and see whether Charity herself can say they believe in the God of Abraham!
entries.7718616f726f73eb8e80c60db3e4ef8ce901a785: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen30451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30452" type="x-p"/> Ye have not obeyed the voice - Though ye have requested to have this particular revelation of the Divine will, and promised obedience, yet have ye not done one thing for which ye sent me to inquire of the Lord.
entries.bff8b31fa76565554e3aa10a8537b5944fb992dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen30452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30453" type="x-p"/> Now therefore know certainly - As ye have determined to disobey, God has determined to punish. Ye may now follow the full bent of your wicked devices, and I will follow the requisitions of my justice. Ye shall die by the sword, by the pestilence, and by the famine, in the place whither ye desire to go to sojourn. Thus was their doom sealed. <div eID="gen30453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30454" type="x-p"/> With such dispositions and with such rebellion of heart, it is strange that they should put themselves to any trouble to inquire of the Lord relative to their future operations. They did not intend to obey; but as a matter of curiosity they would inquire to hear what the prophet might say; and if according to their own inclination, they would obey.  <chapter eID="Jer.42"/> <div eID="gen30454" type="x-p"/>

entries.3bc3aa3156df811ced79d858151d347920564dba: <reference osisRef="Jer.42.1-Jer.42.6">Jer 42:1-6</reference> <hi type="italic">"And there drew near all the captains, namely, Johanan the son of Kareah, and Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah, and all the people, from little to great, </hi> Jer 42:2. <hi type="italic">And said to Jeremiah the prophet, Let our supplication come before thee, and pray for us to Jahveh thy God, for all this remnant (for we are left a few out of many, as thine eyes see us); </hi> Jer 42:3. <hi type="italic">That Jahveh thy God may tell us the way in which we should go, and the thing that we should do."</hi> Of the captains, two, viz., Johanan and Jezaniah, are mentioned as the leaders of the people and the directors of the whole undertaking, who also, Jer 42:1., insolently accuse the prophet of falsehood, and carry out the proposed march to Egypt. Jezaniah is in <reference osisRef="Jer.40.8">Jer 40:8</reference> called the Maachathite; here he is named in connection with his father, "the son of Hoshaiah;" while in <reference osisRef="Jer.43.2">Jer 43:2</reference>, in conjunction with Johanan the son of Kareah, Azariah the son of Hoshaiah is mentioned, which name the lxx also have in <reference osisRef="Jer.42.1">Jer 42:1</reference> of this chapter. Hitzig, Ewald, etc., are consequently of the opinion that יזניה in our verse has been written by mistake for עזריה. But more probable is the supposition that the error is in the עזריה of <reference osisRef="Jer.43.2">Jer 43:2</reference>, inasmuch as there is no reason to doubt the identity of Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah with the Jezaniah descended from Maacha (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.8">Jer 40:8</reference>); and the assumption that יזניה is incorrect in two passages (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.1">Jer 42:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.40.8">Jer 40:8</reference>) is highly improbable. They go to the prophet Jeremiah, whom they had taken with them from Mizpah, where he was living among the people, with the rest of the inhabitants of the place (<reference osisRef="Jer.41.16">Jer 41:16</reference>). תּפּל־נא  as in <reference osisRef="Jer.37.20">Jer 37:20</reference>; see on Jer 36:7. The request made to the prophet that he would intercede for them with the Lord, which they further urge on the ground that the number left out of the whole people is small, while there is implied in this the wish that God may not let this small remnant also perish; - this request Nägelsbach considers a piece of hypocrisy, and the form of asking the prophet "a mere farce," since it is quite plain from <reference osisRef="Jer.43.1-Jer.43.6">Jer 43:1-6</reference> that the desire to go to Egypt was already deeply rooted in their minds, and from this they would not allow themselves to be moved, even by the earnest warning of the prophet. But to hypocrites, who were playing a mere farce with the prophet, the Lord would have probably replied in a different way from what we find in <reference osisRef="Jer.42.8">Jer 42:8</reference>-22. As the Searcher of hearts, He certainly would have laid bare their hypocrisy. And however unequivocally the whole address implies the existence of disobedience to the voice of God, it yet contains nothing which can justify the assumption that it was only in hypocrisy that they wished to learn the will of God. We must therefore assume that their request addressed to the prophet was made in earnest, although they expected that the Lord’s reply would be given in terms favourable to their intention. They wished to obtain from God information as to which way they should go, and what they should do, - not as to whether they should remain in the country or go to Egypt. "The way that we should go" is, of course, not to be understood literally, as if they merely wished to be told the road by which they would most safely reach Egypt; neither, on the other hand, are the words to be understood in a merely figurative sense, of the mode of procedure they ought to pursue; but they are to be understood of the road they ought to take in order to avoid the vengeance of the Chaldeans which they dreaded, - in the sense, whither they ought to go, in order to preserve their lives from the danger which threatened them.
entries.6e2d910660b7e329767bc5eae11286c2370e6420: <reference osisRef="Jer.42.7-Jer.42.11">Jer 42:7-11</reference> <hi type="italic">The word of the Lord.</hi> - At the end of ten days, the reply that had been asked for came from the Lord. Hitzig and Graf think that Jeremiah had lingered ten days with the answer, in order to obtain strong and clear conviction, "matured through his own meditation, probably also in part confirmed by the arrival of further news." This opinion is characterized by Nägelsbach as "in harmony with modern science, but unhistorical;" it should rather be called unscriptural, as resting on a denial of divine inspiration. The reason why the Lord did not make known His will to the prophet for ten days was a disciplinary one. By waiting, those who asked would get time for bethinking themselves, and for quietly considering the situation of affairs, so that they might be able, calmly and collectedly, to receive and obey the answer of God, which was far from satisfying the fears and wishes of their heart. Jer 42:8. Jeremiah called the captains and all the people together, and announced to them as follows: Jer 42:9. <hi type="italic">"Thus saith Jahveh, the God of Israel, to whom ye have sent me, that I might bring your supplication before Him: </hi> Jer 42:10. <hi type="italic">If ye will indeed abide in this land, then will I build you up and not pull down; and I will plant you, but not root out; for I repent of the evil that I have done to you. </hi> Jer 42:11. <hi type="italic">Be not afraid of the king of Babylon, whom ye fear, be not afraid of him, saith Jahveh; for I am with you to save you and to deliver you out of his hand. </hi> Jer 42:12. <hi type="italic">And I will get pity for you, so that he shall take pity on you, and bring you back to your land. </hi> Jer 42:13. <hi type="italic">But if ye say, We will not remain in this land, so that ye will not obey the voice of Jahveh your God, </hi> Jer 42:14. <hi type="italic">Saying, Nay, but we will go to the land of Egypt, that we may not see war nor hear the wound of a trumpet, and we shall not hunger after bread, and we will dwell there. - </hi> Jer 42:15. <hi type="italic">Now therefore hear the word of Jahveh, ye remnant of Judah: Thus saith Jahveh of hosts, the God of Israel, If ye do indeed set your face to go to Egypt, and go to sojourn there, </hi> Jer 42:16. <hi type="italic">Then shall the sword, of which ye are afraid, overtake you there, in the land of Egypt, and hunger, which ye dread, shall there follow hard after you, in Egypt, and there shall ye die. </hi> Jer 42:17. <hi type="italic">And all the men who have set their face to go to Egypt, to sojourn there, shall die by the sword, and through hunger, and from the plague; nor shall they have any one left or escaped from the evil which I will bring on them. </hi> Jer 42:18. <hi type="italic">For thus saith Jahveh of hosts, the God of Israel: As mine anger and my wrath were poured out upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so shall my wrath be poured out upon you when ye go to Egypt, and ye shall become an execration, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach, and ye shall not see this place again. - </hi> Jer 42:19. <hi type="italic">Jahveh hath spoken to you, O remnant of Judah. Go not to Egypt: ye shall know for certain that I have warned you to-day. </hi> Jer 42:20. <hi type="italic">For ye err at the risk of your souls when ye sent me to Jahveh your God, saying, Pray for us to Jahveh our God, and according to all that Jahveh our God shall say to us, so tell us, and we will do it. </hi> Jer 42:21. <hi type="italic">Now I have told you to-day, and ye have not obeyed the voice of Jahveh your God, nor in anything for which He hath sent me unto you. </hi> Jer 42:22. <hi type="italic">Now, therefore, ye must surely know that ye shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence in the place whither ye have been pleased to go to sojourn."</hi> <div eID="gen14323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14324" type="x-p"/> The Lord’s reply extends as far as <reference osisRef="Jer.42.18">Jer 42:18</reference>; the last four verses (19-22) form an epilogue, a further address by the prophet, in which he once more specially impresses God’s resolution on the minds of the people. The answer of God consists (1) in the promise that, if they will remain in the land, the Lord is willing to build them up, and protect them from the wrath of the king of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.9-Jer.42.12">Jer 42:9-12</reference>); and (2) the threat that, if they will go to Egypt against the advice and will of the Lord, they shall certainly perish there by the sword, famine, and pestilence (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.13-Jer.42.18">Jer 42:13-18</reference>). On the expression הפּיל תּהנּה, see on Jer 36:7. שׁוב (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.10">Jer 42:10</reference>) can only be inf. abs. of ישׁב, for ישׁוב ; if we view it as coming from שׁוּב morf , we get no suitable meaning, for the thought <hi type="italic">si revertendo illuc manseritis in hâc terrâ</hi> (C. B. Michaelis) could not be expressed by שׁוב תּשׁבוּ. Certainly there is no other instance of such a form as שׁוב being used for ישׁוב; in a verb like ישׁב, however, which drops the י in the inf. constr., a like omission in the inf. abs. is quite conceivable, while the supposition of some injury having been done to the text (Olshausen, <hi type="italic">Gram</hi>. §89) is less probable. On the expression, "I will build you," etc., cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.24.6">Jer 24:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.4">Jer 31:4</reference>; Jer 33:7. "I repent of the evil" is an anthropopathic expression for the cancelling of a penal sentence: cf. <reference osisRef="Joel.2.14">Joe 2:14</reference>, etc. - In <reference osisRef="Jer.42.11">Jer 42:11</reference>, the repetition of the words "do not fear him" produces special emphasis.
entries.4b06493c570496ac24bf4dd86fed42796915e40b: <reference osisRef="Jer.42.12">Jer 42:12</reference> "I shall give you compassion," i.e., obtain it for you, so that the king of Babylon will show pity on you; cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.43.14">Gen 43:14</reference>; 1Ki 8:50. J. D. Michaelis, Hitzig, Ewald, and Graf, following the lxx, Vulgate, and Syriac, would change והשׁיב into הושׁיב (make you dwell); but there is no necessity for this, since השׁיב makes good enough sense, provided we refer it, not to the return of those who had been exiled to Babylon, but, as the connection requires, to the departure from Mizpah, after the half near Bethlehem, in the intended flight to Egypt; we must, besides, view this departure as a complete forsaking of their country, and the leaders in this emigration as being fugitives who had fled before the Chaldeans, and had returned only a short time before, for the purpose of settling down again in the country.
entries.bad5da612398d8c9c52fcfac3d07efb0523452fc: <reference osisRef="Jer.42.13-Jer.42.16">Jer 42:13-16</reference> <div eID="gen14324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14325" type="x-p"/> The threatening if, in spite of warning and against God’s will, they should still persist in going to Egypt. The protasis of the conditional sentence begun in <reference osisRef="Jer.42.13">Jer 42:13</reference>, "If ye say," etc., extends onwards through <reference osisRef="Jer.42.14">Jer 42:14</reference>; the apodosis is introduced co-ordinately with the commencement of <reference osisRef="Jer.42.15">Jer 42:15</reference>, "Now therefore," etc. קול שׁופר, "the sound of war-trumpet," as in Jer 4:19. On "hungering after bread," cf. Amo 8:11. הלחם (with the article) is the bread necessary for life. "The remnant of Judah" is to be understood of those who still remained in the land, as is shown by <reference osisRef="Jer.42.2">Jer 42:2</reference>; see also <reference osisRef="Jer.42.19">Jer 42:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.43.5">Jer 43:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.44.12">Jer 44:12</reference>, Jer 44:14. The warning given in <reference osisRef="Jer.42.16">Jer 42:16</reference> contains the idea that the very evil which they feared would come on them in Judah will befall them in Egypt. There they shall perish by sword, famine, and plague, since Nebuchadnezzar will conquer Egypt; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.43.8">Jer 43:8</reference>-13.
entries.4d10ec43d37910158088b21ca692294a01a976c7: <reference osisRef="Jer.42.17-Jer.42.22">Jer 42:17-22</reference> ויהיוּ, used instead of the impersonal והיה, is referred to the following subject by a rather unusual kind of attraction; cf. Ewald, §345, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. All the men who set their faces, i.e., intend, to go to Egypt shall perish; not a single one shall escape the evil; for the same judgment of wrath which has befallen Jerusalem shall also come on those who flee to Egypt; cf. Jer 7:20. On the expression "ye shall become a curse," etc., cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.24.9">Jer 24:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.18">Jer 25:18</reference>; Jer 29:18. <div eID="gen14325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14326" type="x-p"/> Taking for granted that the leaders of the people will not obey, Jeremiah appends to the word of the Lord an earnest address, in which several points are specially insisted on, viz., that the Lord had spoken to them, that He had forbidden them to go to Egypt, and that he (the prophet), by proclaiming the word of the Lord, had warned them (העיד בּ, to testify, bear witness against a person, i.e., warn him of something, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.11.7">Jer 11:7</reference>). Thus he discloses to them the dangerous mistake they are in, when they first desire some expression of the mind of the Lord regarding their intentions, and, in the hope that He will accede to their request, promise unconditional obedience to whatever He may direct, but afterwards, when they have received a message from the Lord, will not obey it, because it is contrary to what they wish. The <hi type="italic">Kethib</hi> התעתים has been incorrectly written for התעיים, the Hiphil from תּעה, to <hi type="italic">err</hi>; here, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.10.17">Pro 10:17</reference>, it means to make a mistake. בּנפשׁותיכם, not, "you mislead <hi type="italic">your own selves</hi>," <hi type="italic">decepistis animas vestras</hi> (Vulg.), nor "in your souls," - meaning, in your thoughts and intentions (Nägelsbach), - but "at the risk of your souls," your life; cf. Jer 17:21. וּלכל אשׁר (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.21">Jer 42:21</reference>), "and that in regard to all that for which Jahveh has sent me to you," points back to their promise, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.5">Jer 42:5</reference>, that they would do "according to all the word." By employing the perfect in <reference osisRef="Jer.42.20">Jer 42:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.42.21">Jer 42:21</reference>, the thing is represented as quite certain, as if it had already taken place. <reference osisRef="Jer.42.22">Jer 42:22</reference> concludes the warning with a renewed threat of the destruction which shall befall them for their disobedience.  <chapter eID="Jer.42"/> <div eID="gen14326" type="x-p"/>

entries.21e3a2cd3d05e30f0109fe87ec8202811eb1e5c9: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.42.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jer.42.1" sID="gen63974" type="section"/> <div sID="gen63975" type="x-p"/>I have said that John, and his associates, and the whole people acted much more culpably by coming to the Prophet, than if they had not done so, and had gone directly to Egypt: for they either came dissemblingly, and thus designedly spoke what was false, or they were extremely stupid, and hypocrisy had wholly deprived them of their understanding. They came to the Prophet to ask counsel; nay, that he might be to them God’s interpreter, and that thus they might know what to do; and they promised to obey, as we shall hereafter see. However this may have been, they sought an oracle in which it was their duty to acquiesce, except they resolved openly to shake off the yoke and to show themselves to be gross and profane despisers of God. They came to the Prophet, when yet it was their fixed purpose, as we shall see, to go to Egypt.<div eID="gen63975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen63976" type="x-p"/>He who asks counsel, ought first to see that he bring no prejudice, but be free and honest: but it is, however, a fault too common, that men deliberate and ask counsel, when they have already settled what to do; nay, nothing is more common than this; for those who consult do not, for the most part, wish to learn what is right, but that others should fall in with their own inclinations. He who has resolved on this or that point, pretends that he is in doubt, and held in suspense; he asks what ought to be done: if the answer be according to his wishes, he embraces what is said; but if he who is consulted, disapproves of what he has already resolved to do, he rejects the counsel given. Such was the dissimulation described by the Prophet, when the leaders of the forces and the whole people came to him.<div eID="gen63976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen63977" type="x-p"/>He mentions, first, the <hi type="italic">leaders of the forces, </hi>and then <hi type="italic">John the son of Kareah, and Jezaniah the son of Hoshiah</hi> He adds these two last; but it was to give them honor, as when the angel said,<div eID="gen63977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen63978" type="x-p"/>“Go and tell his disciples and Peter.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.16.7">Mark 16:7</reference>)<div eID="gen63978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen63979" type="x-p"/>He did not put aside Peter, as though he was inferior to all the rest; but for the sake of honor he mentions his name, after having spoken generally of them all. So also here, the Prophet names generally the <hi type="italic">leaders, </hi>but as John the son of Kareah, and Jezaniah were the chief men, he expressly gives their names. He adds, the whole people, <hi type="italic">from the least to the greatest</hi> This does not refer to age; but what he means is, that all, of every grade, came with one consent to Jeremiah. It was not then the conspiring of a few men, but all from the least to the greatest had resolved to go to Egypt; and yet they came, as though with an honest purpose, to the Prophet; wherefore? They wished their own perverse design to be approved by God, and thus to subject God to their own will and humor; for they did not suffer themselves to be ruled by his Spirit, but audaciously disregarded his word. The Prophet then shews that they were all implicated in the same sin.<div eID="gen63979" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.42.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen63974" osisID="Jer.42.1" type="section"/>
entries.c209e25fd265975041c9bb032436c5681f0e5085: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.42.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jer.42.2" sID="gen63980" type="section"/> <div sID="gen63981" type="x-p"/>It is added, that they <hi type="italic">said, </hi>as though they were ready to obey, <hi type="italic">Let our prayer fall before thee.</hi> This, as we have said, when addressed to God, is an <hi type="italic">evidence </hi>of humility; but it is applied here to man; and when the Hebrews make a humble request, they say, “Let my prayer fall before <hi type="italic">thee,” </hi>that is, Hear what I suppliantly and humbly ask. <hi type="italic">Pray, </hi>they said, <hi type="italic">to Jehovah thy God for us</hi> They called him the God of Jeremiah, not that they intended to exempt themselves from his authority; they did not mean that they were alienated from God; but in this way they extolled Jeremiah, and acknowledged him to be God’s true and lawful Prophet. In short, this saying refers to the prophetic office, as though they had said, that Jeremiah had hitherto confirmed his vocation, so that it was clearly evident that he had been sent from above.<div eID="gen63981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen63982" type="x-p"/>We hence see why they called Jehovah the <hi type="italic">God </hi>of Jeremiah, not as though they had rejected God, and as though he was not their God in common with Jeremiah, but they allowed that the Prophet possessed a higher honor, and that his faithfulness and integrity were beyond controversy.<div eID="gen63982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen63983" type="x-p"/>But this admission justly recoiled on their own head; for if Jeremiah was God’s Prophet, why did they not instantly obey him, after knowing that what he faithfully told them he had received from God? and why did they insolently and ferociously resist him and accuse him of falsehood? Their own admission then was not sincere, but a fallacious flattery, as is the case with all hypocrites, who never speak in sincerity and truth.<div eID="gen63983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen63984" type="x-p"/>They afterwards added, <hi type="italic">Pray for all this remnant, for we are left, a few from many</hi> This they added to produce pity, in order that they might more easily obtain from Jeremiah what they asked; nor was that difficult; but as they felt conscious of wrong, they sought the favor of the Prophet by flatteries, Had they asked him without disguise, they knew that he was of himself disposed to seek the well being of the people; but as they were of a double mind, they set before him their miserable state, which might; have roused the Prophet still more to make intercession to God for them. And for this reason they added, <hi type="italic">as thine eyes see us</hi> And they set before him this sad spectacle, to create sympathy in the Prophet. And it then follows, And <hi type="italic">may Jehovah thy God shew us the way in which we are to walk. </hi>They now explained more clearly why they wished prayer to be made for them, even that God might answer and shew what he wished them to do.<div eID="gen63984" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.42.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen63980" osisID="Jer.42.2" type="section"/>
entries.8773450fff19537e2b93e90ba3a15ffd385593e3:
They came then, as it has been stated, as though they were ready to obey; and then they professed humility, because they did not wish to do anything rashly, but only to follow where God called them. Had they spoken from the heart, it would have been a rare virtue thus to-have fled in perplexities to God, and to have allowed themselves to be ruled by his word; but we shall see that it was all a pre-tence. We have then here set before us the hypocrisy of that people, so that we may learn that whenever we ask what pleases God, we should bring a pure and sincere heart, so that nothing may prevent or hinder us immediately to embrace whatever God may command us. But their hypocrisy is discovered to have been still baser, when the Prophet adds,
Jeremiah 42:4
4. Then Jeremiah the prophet said unto them, I have heard you; behold, I will pray unto the LORD your God according to your words; and it shall come to pass, that whatsoever thing the LORD shall answer you, I will declare it unto you; I will keep nothing back from you.
4. Et dixit illis Jeremias Propheta, Audivi, ecce ego orabo Jehovam Deum vestrum secundum sermones vestros, et erit quemcunque sermonem responderit Jehova vobis, annuntiabo vobis, non celabo a vobis quicquam.
entries.936b255fe29c4af743b070c34b3b9995c75c0c28:
In order to prepare them to obey, he testified that he would be a faithful messenger of God; for there is no doubt but that the Prophet, as we shall see, regarded them with suspicion. That he might therefore have them teachable and obedient to the answer expected from God, he said beforehand, that he would honestly and faithfully perform his office as a Prophet.
I have heard, he says; here he shews how ready he was to attend, and how he neglected nothing conducive to their well being. I have heard, he says, Behold, I will pray according to your words There is no doubt but that he thus intimated that he wished well to them; and it might have rendered them more attentive to the oracle to know that the Prophet was influenced by love. Nor is there a doubt but that the Prophet testified his love towards them, that his doctrine might afterwards have more weight with them.
By saying, Whatever your God will answer, he did not mean that the oracle would be revealed to all, for the words could not be otherwise explained than through the Prophet, who would openly make known to the whole people what he heard from God’s mouth. But he says, that the answer would be given to them, because God would give the answer which was to be communicated to all, as it is said that God spoke to Moses, and also to all the people, for the doctrine was intended for all. Moses did not receive the law, nor its interpretation, in his own private character, but in order that the people might know what was right. So Jeremiah did here; the answer he received from God he made known as belonging in common to all the people.
But in calling God their God, he did not mean to flatter them or to praise their piety, but to exhort them to surrender and devote themselves wholly to God, as though he had said, that they had to do with God, who had bound them to himself when he adopted them as his peculiar people, and then favored them with so many blessings. Since then God had made himself known to them, they could not reject his counsel with impunity, for there was no pretext of ignorance. We hence see what weight there is in this, your God; for Jeremiah reminded them that they could not with impunity trifle with God, for they were not their own, but had been chosen to be God’s people, and on this condition, to be wholly subject to his authority. Then the sum of the whole is this, that the Prophet would faithfully convey to the Jews the answer God would give them; and he said this that his doctrine might have a greater authority among them. It now follows, —
Jeremiah 42:5-6
5. Then they said to Jeremiah, The LORD be a true and faithful witness between us, if we do not even according to all things for the which the LORD thy God shall send thee to us.
5. Ipsi antem dixerunt ad Jeremiam, Erit Jehova inter nos in testem (vel, testis) fidei et veritatis (testis fidelis et verax,) nisi secundum omnem sermonem quem miserit (id est, pro quo miserit) Jehova Deus tuus ad nos, sic facturi sumus;
6. Whether it be good, or whether it be evil, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God, to whom we send thee; that it may be well with us, when we obey the voice of the LORD our God.
6. Sive bonum, sive malum, voci Jehovae Dei nostri, pro qua nos mittimus te ad ipsum, obediemus (audiemus vocem, ad verbum, sed tantundem valet, audire vocem atque obedire voci,) ut bene sit nobis, cum obediverimus voci Dei nostri.
entries.ccea67250ca58ddcacaf7e638143695afe2a89f5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.42.5" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Jer.42.5" sID="gen64004" type="section"/> <div sID="gen64005" type="x-p"/>It hence appears that the people understood for what purpose Jeremiah, before he consulted God, assured them of his faithfulness and sincerity; for it was not without reason that they promised to be obedient to God; but as they saw that they were suspected as being not sincere by Jeremiah, and as he had promised to be a true and faithful teacher, they on the other hand declared that they would be sincere disciples, and would receive whatever God might command them. But they soon betrayed their perfidy, for when they heard that what they had resolved to do did not please God, they not only rejected the counsel of God and the Prophet, but treated him insolently, and even loaded the holy man with reproaches, as though he had told them what was false. Their hypocrisy ought at the same time to be a lesson to us, so that when God is pleased through a singular favor to shew us the way of acting rightly by faithful instructors and competent teachers, we may not be like them, but be teachable and ready to obey, and prove this not only by the mouth but also by our deeds.<div eID="gen64005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen64006" type="x-p"/>The Prophet then says, that they spoke thus, <hi type="italic">Let God be a faithful and true witness between us.</hi> Being not content with a simple affirmation, they dared to interpose the name of God; and thus we see how blind is hypocrisy. For if men duly weigh what it is to profane God’s name, surely they would dread and abominate all perjury. As then they rushed on so audaciously to swear, it is evident that they were as it were stupefied; and there is no inebriety which so confuses the minds of men and all their senses as hypocrisy.<div eID="gen64006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen64007" type="x-p"/>They then added, <hi type="italic">According to whatever word which Jehovah thy God shall send to us, so will we do,</hi> that is, whatever Jehovah shall command us by thee; for God is said to send to men, when he sends a messenger in his name to bring his commands. Jeremiah then was, as it were, a middle person to address the people in God’s name, as though he had been sent from heaven. They therefore said, that they would do whatever God commanded. A stronger expression follows, <hi type="italic">Whether good or evil, we will obey the voice of Jehovah our God</hi> They did not here charge God’s word with being wrong, as though it had anything unjust in it; but they used <hi type="italic">good </hi>in the sense of joyful, and <hi type="italic">evil </hi>as meaning what is sad or grievous, as though they had said, that they asked for no other thing but that God should declare what pleased him, and that they were so submissive as to refuse nothing though contrary to the flesh. Had this declaration proceeded from the heart, it would have been a testimony of true piety; for the minds of the godly ought to be so framed as to obey God without making any exception, whether he commands what is contrary to their purpose, or leads them where they do not wish to go; for they who wish to make a compact with God, that he should require nothing but what is agreeable to them, shew that they know not what it is to serve God. Hence the obedience of faith in an especial manner requires this, that man should <hi type="italic">renounce </hi>his own desires, that he should not set up his own counsels and wishes against the word of God, nor object and say, this is hard, that is not quite agreeable. <hi type="italic">Whether </hi>then <hi type="italic">it be good </hi>or <hi type="italic">evil, </hi>that is, though it may be contrary to the feelings of the flesh, we ought still to embrace what God requires and commands: this is the rule of true religion.<div eID="gen64007" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Jer.42.5" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen64004" osisID="Jer.42.5" type="section"/>
entries.106867083ec9920090228dea850197f5f4e5069b:
As the Jews spoke feignedly by assuming a character not their own, they profaned God’s name. But if we desire to prove our fidelity to God, the only way of acting is, to regard his word as binding, whether it be agreeable or otherwise, and never to murmur, as the ungodly do; for when God would have a yoke laid on them, they complain that his doctrine is too hard and burdensome. Away, then, with all those things which can render God’s word unacceptable to us, if we desire to give a sure proof of our fidelity. Hence they said, Whether it be good or evil, what God will lay down we will obey his voice.
They afterwards added, For which we send thee to him
Our version is, “to whom we send thee,” and correctly too: literally it is, “whom we send thee to him,” an idiom common in Hebrew and also in Welsh, “yr hwn y danfonwn di atto.” The Vulg. is, “to whom we send thee;” and so in the Syriac. and Targum., but the Septuagint tried to imitate the Hebrew, and there is no sense given. — Ed.
Here they still further cast themselves into toils. Jeremiah did not in express words require them to make an oath; they yet did make an oath; and then in various ways still more bound themselves over to punishment, if they became perjurers. They now shew that it would be a two-fold crime, should they disobey God; how? Had the Prophet been sent to them, they might have made excuses; though vain, they might yet have something to allege; but when they of their own accord asked God, when they offered of themselves to do this, and promised to be obedient in all things, it is evident that unless afterwards they acted according to their pledged faith, they must have been more inexcusable, because they tempted God: for who induced them to come to the Prophet? We hence see that God extorted from them what doubled their crime. But the more hypocrites attempt by disguises to conceal their impiety, the faster they bind themselves, and the more they kindle God’s wrath against themselves.
They then added, That it may be well with us when we obey the voice of Jehovah By this circumstance also they aggravated their crime. For if the Prophet had promised them a prosperous issue, they might not have believed; in that case they would have indeed sinned; but their wicked-ness would have been more tolerable than when they themselves had spoken, as though they were the organs of the Holy Spirit; they said themselves, It shall be well with us; it will be our chief happiness to follow the voice of God and to obey him. As, then, they thus protested to God and the Prophet, that they might appear to be God’s faithful servants, the greater condemnation they brought on themselves; for if they believed that nothing would turn out happily, except according to God’s command, how was it that they did not submit to God? why did they despise what was afterwards said by the Prophet?
